chapter: The House That Jazz Built and Homestead childhood
title: Local bands, Local 471 and Pittsburgh halls, theaters and parks
summary: Swing bands at the Pythian Temple, Syria Mosque, Kennywood Park, and Pittsburgh theaters including burlesque and legitimate houses.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Benny Goodman, you know, the Swing era had begun. And the William Penn Hotel, Count Basie was the first Black band to go into the William Penn Hotel. This was on account of John Hammond, I suppose.

But around Pittsburgh proper there were quite a few local bands that played at dances and some of the big affairs there. Around Pittsburgh there there was definitely a time between when you had a Black local and a white local. There was the Musicians Club in Pittsburgh, up on Wylie Avenue, which was headquarters, I suppose, for the local at that time.
Was it the local I mentioned before?
Yeah, Local 471, yeah, in Pittsburgh and that was the Black local and that's where most of the musicians would hang out.

Of course there were halls in Pittsburgh and Homestead, for that matter, that local promoters would rent, you know, to have dances. Then they built a club out in East End called The Savoy Ballroom where most of the bands used to come, and of course, in the early days before the Savoy Ballroom was built they

I've also seen the Loew's
Vaudeville Theater.

Loew's -- I only played
Loew's when I came to New York.

No, this is in Pittsburgh.
It's in the book on Earl Hines.

There was a Loew's --
yeah, Pittsburgh had a lot of theaters -- Warner
Brothers Theater. Dick Powell was the M.C. and singer at
the Warner Brothers Theater for years and Loew's of
course, the RKO Keith. They had two burlesque houses,
the Academy and the Gaiety and in fact my uncle, my
grandmother's brother used to take me to matinees to

a burlesque theater when they'd have a mixed bill down there. He would take me down to either one of the burlesque houses. Because the burlesque houses were the only ones that had probably mixed companies.

Then we had our legitimate theaters, the Nixon Theater which some of the shows like "Blackbirds" and "Connie's Hot Chocolates" played Pittsburgh and then in East Liberty -- now this was in Pittsburgh off Wylie Avenue where they had a theater, the Elmore Theater and they brought a lot of Black productions to the Elmore Theater.
Troupes like Butterbeans and Susie and her troop. the Whitman Sisters and whatever group was on the road at the time. So I was exposed to a lot of theater and music.
